name: Operations in the District AI Policy
title: Operations in the District AI Policy
answer: A district AI policy should cover operations tools, not only classroom tools, because buses, meals and similar services make decisions that affect students every day. The same principles of privacy, human review and verified results that apply in classrooms should apply to those tools. A simple inventory of operations tools shows the board where those protections exist and where they are missing.

sections.body: District AI policies tend to be written with classrooms in mind, and operations tools are often left out of them. That gap matters because operations tools make daily decisions about students, from how bus routes are drawn to how meal portions are set. The book argues that the district policy should treat operations tools under the same principles it applies elsewhere, namely privacy, human review and verified results. The elements of a sound policy were set out earlier in the book, in Chapter 3, and they are meant to carry across the district rather than stop at the classroom door. The problem this solves is a policy that looks complete while leaving a whole set of student-affecting decisions unexamined.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide this work by grade band, because operations decisions apply across the whole district rather than to one age group. What it recommends is an inventory. The district lists every operations tool that uses AI, the decisions each one supports, who reviews its output, and what data it uses. That list shows where human review and privacy protections are already in place and where they are missing. It also gives the board a clear picture of how AI is actually being used in operations.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a research evidence label to this idea. What it offers instead is a legal and policy context: Texas's AI governance law defines covered government entities broadly enough to include school districts, and it took effect in January 2026 (Texas Legislature, 2025). Ohio requires every district to adopt an AI policy, and its state model policy is available to guide districts (Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, 2026). The text adds that districts should confirm their own obligations with counsel. Beyond these references, the case for covering operations tools rests on practice rather than on studies reported in the text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits the text sets concern who still decides. Human review, privacy protection and verified results are the conditions it names, and the inventory exists to reveal where those conditions are absent. The decisions themselves stay with people rather than with the tools. Legal obligations vary, and the text is explicit that districts should confirm what applies to them with counsel. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
